why.correct: Heat from Earth's interior makes mantle rock slowly rise, spread and sink. These convection currents drag the rigid plates above them.
options: Right: hot mantle rock rises, cools and sinks, and the moving mantle carries the plates.
Seawater pushes on rock only weakly, far too weakly to move a plate.
The Moon raises tides, but it does not drive plate motion.
Winds move air and water at the surface; plates are rock about 100 km thick.

why.correct: Two continents collide. Continental crust is too light to sink far, so the crust crumples and stacks up into very high mountains.
options: Right: the plates move toward each other, and the crust folds into mountains.
Spreading plates form ridges and rift valleys, not the highest mountains on Earth.
At a transform boundary the plates slide past each other; they do not push crust upward this much.
A hot spot forms volcanoes in the middle of a plate, not a long mountain range at a plate edge.

why.correct: The hot spot stays in place deep below. The plate slides over it, carrying each finished volcano away, so the oldest islands are farthest from the hot spot.
options: Right: the plate carries older volcanoes northwest, away from the hot spot.
Transform boundaries cause earthquakes; they do not build a line of volcanoes that get older in one direction.
A spreading boundary would make rock older in both directions, away from a central ridge.
Hawaii is in the middle of the Pacific Plate, far from any plate boundary.

why.correct: At a transform boundary the plates grind past each other. Stress builds and is released as earthquakes, but no plate sinks and little magma rises.
options: Right: the Pacific Plate slides past the North American Plate.
A divergent boundary would let magma rise and form new crust, with volcanic activity.
Subduction makes trenches and chains of volcanoes, which this fault does not have.
A collision of continents builds high mountain ranges, not a long sliding fault.

why.correct: Subduction zones surround much of the Pacific. A sinking plate causes strong earthquakes, and the rock above it melts to feed volcanoes.
options: Right: the ring follows convergent boundaries with subduction.
Depth of the ocean does not cause the pattern; the boundaries do.
Hot spots make lines of volcanoes in the middle of plates, not a ring at their edges.
Seawater does not melt rock; magma comes from deep below the crust.

why.correct: Where the denser ocean plate sinks, the seafloor bends down into a trench, and the melting rock above the sinking plate feeds volcanoes, as in the Andes.
options: Right: the sinking plate forms a trench.
Right: rock above the sinking plate melts, and the magma rises to form volcanoes.
A rift valley forms where plates pull apart, at a divergent boundary.
A mid-ocean ridge forms where ocean plates move apart, not where they collide.

why.correct: At a divergent boundary the gap between plates lets hot mantle rock rise. As it rises the pressure on it drops, it partly melts, and the magma fills the gap as new crust.
options: Right: pulling apart lets mantle rock rise, melt and form new crust.
Sinking describes a convergent boundary; at a ridge the plates move apart.
Sliding past each other describes a transform boundary, which has few volcanoes.
Water pressure does not melt rock; the magma comes from rising mantle rock.

why.correct: A sudden slip moves the seafloor, which moves the whole column of water above it; that water spreads as tsunami waves.
Arrows pointing apart mark a divergent boundary. Rising magma fills the gap and builds a ridge of new crust.
options: Right: the boundary is divergent, with magma rising between the plates.
Colliding plates are shown in the middle, where one plate sinks.
Sliding plates are shown in the inset seen from above.
The diagram shows the magma at a plate edge, not under the middle of a plate.

why.correct: Ocean crust is made of dense basalt; continental crust is lighter. When they meet, the denser plate sinks into the mantle.
options: Right: the denser plate sinks below the lighter one.
Ocean crust is thinner than continental crust, not thicker.
The water above is not what makes the plate sink; the rock is denser.
Speed does not decide which plate sinks; density does.

why.correct: The sinking plate carries water down with it. Heat and that water make the mantle rock above it melt, and the light magma rises to form volcanoes.
options: Right: melting above the sinking plate feeds the volcanoes.
The ridge is a separate boundary; its magma does not travel under the ocean to the continent.
The transform boundary in the inset is not connected to this volcano.
Water helps rock melt, but the volcano erupts magma, not boiling seawater.

why.correct: A subduction zone produces some of the strongest earthquakes on Earth, and the melting plate feeds explosive volcanoes, as along the Andes and in Japan.
options: Right: subduction brings both strong earthquakes and volcanoes.
Rift valleys form where plates pull apart, not where they collide.
Hurricanes form over warm ocean water; plate motion does not cause them.
The grinding and sudden slipping of the sinking plate causes frequent earthquakes too.

why.correct: Distance and age rise together in a straight line. New crust forms at the ridge and is carried away as more forms behind it: seafloor spreading.
options: Right: both values rise together, so older rock is farther away.
The age changes with distance; it is 0 at the ridge and 4 million years at 100 km.
The newest rock, age 0, is at the ridge, so rock gets older moving away.
The line is straight, so the age keeps rising at the same rate with distance.

why.correct: Soil forms where rock is broken down into mineral particles by weathering and dead plants and animals decay into humus, mixing over long periods.
options: Right: weathered rock supplies minerals, and decayed organisms supply humus.
Erosion removes soil; it does not form it where it starts.
Roots do not photosynthesize, and evaporation does not make soil.
Compaction damages soil, and bedrock is not melted at the surface.

why.correct: Chemical weathering and the work of decomposers both speed up when it is warm and wet. Cold, frozen tundra slows both.
options: Right: climate controls how fast rock weathers and dead matter decays.
The question says the rock is the same kind, so rock type is not the difference.
Tundra plants grow slowly and add little organic matter, and more organic matter would build soil, not slow it.
Wind erosion removes soil; rainforests are also sheltered from wind by trees.

why.correct: Humus is what is left when decomposers break down dead plants and animals. It darkens topsoil, holds water and supplies nutrients.
options: Right: humus is broken-down organic matter.
Solid rock under soil is bedrock, the parent material.
Clay collects in the B horizon, but it is mineral matter, not humus.
Water in soil is not humus, though humus helps soil hold water.

why.correct: Roots bind soil particles together and leaves and stalks shield the surface. Plowing breaks up the soil and leaves it bare, so wind can lift it.
options: Right: bare, loose soil has nothing holding it down.
Plowing turns plant matter under; it does not make the soil lighter.
Grass slows the wind at the ground; it does not speed it up.
Ordinary plowing turns the topsoil, not the deep C horizon.

why.correct: Each link has to be named: roots gone, more soil eroded by rain, more sediment in the river, then the harm to the river.
The A horizon is topsoil: humus mixed with mineral particles. It is dark and full of roots, worms and microbes.
options: Right: topsoil is the A horizon.
The B horizon is subsoil, where minerals leached from above collect.
The C horizon is partly weathered parent material with little humus.
The O horizon is mostly undecayed leaves and organic matter above the mineral soil.

why.correct: Rain soaks into the soil and dissolves or carries fine particles and minerals downward. They build up in the subsoil: this is leaching.
options: Right: water moving down leaches minerals into the B horizon.
Roots take minerals up from the soil, the opposite direction.
Wind moves surface soil; it does not move minerals down through the profile.
Heat from bedrock does not move minerals in a soil profile.

why.correct: Soil forms from both directions: rock weathers from below and organic matter is added from above. The C horizon is near the rock and far from the leaves at the surface.
options: Right: the C horizon is mostly partly weathered parent material.
Humus is light; it stays in the upper horizons.
Decomposers break down dead organic matter, not rock.
Wind reaches only the surface, not deep horizons.

why.correct: If a few centimeters take centuries to form, losing 1 cm a year removes in a few years what took centuries to build. Topsoil is a resource that renews too slowly to keep up.
options: Right: the loss far outpaces formation.
Formation is far slower than 1 cm a year.
Erosion does not speed up soil formation enough to replace the loss.
Roots and nutrients are mostly in the topsoil, the A horizon, not the C horizon.

why.correct: Soil loss rises from 0.4 to 30.0 metric tons per hectare as cover goes from never-plowed grass to bare, plowed soil.
options: Right: bare ground loses the most soil, grass the least.
The plowed plots (3 and 4) lose the most soil.
Losses range from 0.4 to 30.0 metric tons per hectare, a large difference.
The plot with stalks loses less than the bare, plowed plots.

Keeping the stalks on the field cuts soil loss by about 79%.

<math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>30.0</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mfrac><mtext>metric tons</mtext><mtext>ha</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>40</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ha</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30.0\,\frac{\text{metric tons}}{\text{ha}} \times 40\,\text{ha}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 1{,}200</annotation></semantics></math> metric tons. The hectares cancel.
The more cover the ground keeps, the less soil it loses: grass loses 0.4, stalks 2.5, a crop on bare soil 12.0 and bare soil 30.0 metric tons per hectare.
options: Right: every step toward more cover lowers soil loss.
Bare soil with no crop (30.0) loses more than a crop on plowed soil (12.0), not less.
The plowed plots lose far more soil than the unplowed grass.
Native grass loses the least, 0.4 metric tons per hectare.

why.correct: The farmer links plowing (no grass roots) and drought to wind erosion, and describes the poor wheat that grew afterward.
options: Right: the passage ties plowing and drought to the loss of topsoil.
The passage says the plowed field lost its topsoil, the opposite of good growth.
The farmer stresses that there were no grass roots to hold the soil, not drought alone.
The problem was dry years, not a wet climate.

why.correct: Thin, short wheat where the topsoil blew away is evidence that the subsoil left behind grows crops poorly.
options: Right: poor growth on the exposed subsoil is the evidence of harm.
Good rain and prices describe the years before the loss.
Plowing explains the cause, not the harm.
Keeping stalks is the farmer's response, not evidence of the harm.

why.correct: The contrast between "his life" and "a few seasons" rests on the idea that soil forms slowly, over centuries, while it can be lost quickly.
options: Right: the sentence contrasts slow formation with fast loss.
Planting does not make soil quickly; soil forms from weathering and decay over centuries.
The passage describes poor wheat on the subsoil, the opposite.
The passage describes the wind carrying soil away, not bringing it back.

why.correct: Sand grains are the largest (up to 2 mm), silt is medium, and clay particles are the smallest (less than 0.002 mm).
options: Right: sand is largest and clay smallest.
This is smallest to largest, the reverse order.
Sand grains are larger than silt.
Clay particles are smaller than silt.

why.correct: Permeability depends on pore size. Large sand grains leave large, connected pores; tiny clay particles leave tiny pores that water moves through slowly.
options: Right: big, connected pores make sand highly permeable.
Humus does not pull water down; sand usually holds little humus.
Clay particles are the smallest, not the largest.
Clay has plenty of pore space, but its pores are tiny, so water moves slowly through them.

why.correct: Loam mixes sand, silt and clay, so it combines enough drainage and air space with enough water-holding capacity and nutrients.
options: Right: loam balances drainage and water-holding capacity.
Sand drains so fast that it holds little water for plants.
Clay holds water but drains slowly, so roots can run short of air.
Silty clay is mostly fine particles, so it drains slowly too.

why.correct: Tiny clay particles and humus have huge surface areas that hold nutrients, and humus releases nutrients as it decays. Water washes nutrients through sand quickly.
options: Right: clay and humus hold onto nutrients.
Clay and humus slow water down; sand drains fastest.
Sand is not poisonous; it just holds few nutrients.
Fertility is about nutrients, not soil temperature.

why.correct: A pH below 7 is acidic; 4.5 is strongly acidic. Most crops grow best near pH 6 to 7, and at low pH some nutrients become hard for roots to take up while some metals become more soluble.
options: Right: pH 4.5 is strongly acidic and limits nutrients.
Neutral is pH 7, not 4.5.
Basic soils have a pH above 7; pH also does not set how much water soil holds.
pH does not measure humus or fertility directly.

why.correct: Sand, silt and clay add to 100%: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>%</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\% - (35\% + 45\%) = 20\%</annotation></semantics></math> clay. That sample is a loam.
Sample B (40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay) sits inside the shaded loam region in the middle of the triangle.
options: Right: B is in the loam region.
Sample A is in the sandy clay loam region.
Sample C is in the clay region at the top.
Sample D is in the silt loam region.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>74</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\% - (6\% + 20\%) = 74\%</annotation></semantics></math> silt, which is why D sits in the silt loam region.
Sample C is 60% clay. Clay's tiny pores hold water tightly and pass it slowly, so C has high water-holding capacity and low permeability.
options: Right: the clay sample holds water and drains slowly.
Sample A is 70% sand, so it drains quickly.
Sample B is a loam, in between.
Sample D is mostly silt with little clay, so it holds less water than C.

why.correct: A drain field needs water to soak in. Sample C, 60% clay, has low permeability, so wastewater would back up and pool.
options: Right: the clay sample has the lowest permeability.
Loam drains at a moderate rate, which suits a drain field.
Sand drains quickly; it does not hold water tightly.
Silt has pore space; it drains more slowly than sand but much faster than clay.

why.correct: Clay took 50 minutes and held 110 mL; sand took 2 minutes and held 30 mL. Slow drainage and high water-holding go together.
options: Right: slow drainage goes with more water held.
Sand held the least water (30 mL) and drained fastest (2 minutes).
Water held ranged from 30 mL to 110 mL, a big difference.
Clay drained the least water out (90 mL).

The minutes cancel.

<math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>110</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mL</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>200</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mL</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{110\,\text{mL}}{200\,\text{mL}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>55</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 55\%</annotation></semantics></math>.

why.correct: A hypothesis is a statement with a direction that names the variable measured: drainage time.
The troposphere, the lowest layer, holds about three quarters of the air's mass and nearly all its water vapor, so clouds, rain and storms form there.
options: Right: weather happens in the troposphere.
The stratosphere is dry and stable; it holds the ozone layer.
The mesosphere is far above the clouds.
The thermosphere is extremely thin air, far above the weather.

why.correct: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most UV-B and nearly all UV-C, which would otherwise damage DNA, cause skin cancer and cataracts, and harm plants and plankton.
options: Right: the ozone layer filters out most harmful UV radiation.
Keeping Earth warm is a different job, done mostly by gases such as water vapor and carbon dioxide in the troposphere.
The oxygen animals breathe is O2 made by photosynthesis, not ozone.
Ozone absorbs UV light; it does not act as a mirror for sunlight.

why.correct: As ozone absorbs UV light, it warms the air around it. The most absorption is in the upper stratosphere, so temperature climbs with height.
options: Right: ozone absorbing UV heats the stratosphere.
A few kilometers is nothing compared with the 150 million km to the Sun.
Air rising from the ground cools as it rises and stops at the top of the troposphere.
The stratosphere is too dry for ordinary clouds.

why.correct: Sunlight warms the ground, which warms the air above it. Air that rises meets lower pressure, expands and cools, so the troposphere cools by about 6.5 °C per kilometer on average.
options: Right: heating from below plus cooling of rising air makes the troposphere colder with height.
The ozone layer is where the air starts to warm, not a cold source.
Mountain peaks get plenty of sunlight.
The share of oxygen stays about 21% with height; the air just gets thinner.

why.correct: The drop is <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>6.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mfrac><mtext>°C</mtext><mtext>km</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>km</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.5\,\frac{\text{°C}}{\text{km}} \times 3\,\text{km}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>19.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>°C</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 19.5\,\text{°C}</annotation></semantics></math>, so the peak is <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>19.5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>°C</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20 - 19.5 = 0.5\,\text{°C}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Ozone (O3) is the same molecule everywhere. High up it absorbs UV light before it reaches the surface; at ground level it is a pollutant people and plants take in.
options: Right: the same molecule, different effects depending on location.
Both are O3, the same molecule.
Breathing ozone harms lung tissue; it is not harmless.
The harm near the ground comes from breathing ozone, not from UV absorption.

why.correct: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. The ozone layer lies about 15 to 35 km up, in the stratosphere. Most of the air's mass is in the troposphere.
options: Right: nitrogen is about 78% of dry air.
The ozone layer is in the stratosphere, above the troposphere.
The thermosphere holds a tiny fraction of the air; about 75% of the mass is in the troposphere.
Oxygen is about 21% of dry air, not half.

why.correct: The line slopes from 15 °C at 0 km to −56.5 °C at 11 km. This lowest layer, where temperature falls with height, is the troposphere.
options: Right: temperature falls with height in the troposphere.
−56.5 °C is colder than 15 °C, so temperature falls.
The line moves left (colder) as altitude rises.
That pattern describes the whole graph up to 85 km, not the first 11 km.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>56.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>°C</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>°C</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>km</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{-56.5\,\text{°C} - 15\,\text{°C}}{11\,\text{km}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>71.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>°C</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>11</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>km</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{-71.5\,\text{°C}}{11\,\text{km}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>6.5</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>°C/km</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -6.5\,\text{°C/km}</annotation></semantics></math>. Temperature falls 6.5 °C for each kilometer.
From about 11 to 50 km is the stratosphere. Its ozone absorbs ultraviolet light, so it warms with height.
options: Right: ozone in the stratosphere absorbs UV and warms the air.
The troposphere ends near 11 km and cools with height.
The mesosphere, above 50 km, cools with height.

why.correct: Storm clouds grow while rising air stays warmer and lighter than the air around it. Where temperature stops falling and then rises, rising air quickly matches its surroundings and stops climbing.
options: Right: the change in the temperature trend at 11 km caps rising air.

−56.5 °C at 11 km is one of the coldest points on the graph.
The graph continues to 85 km; the air is thin but present.

why.correct: Oxygen is 20.95%, about 21 of every 100 molecules, which is roughly one fifth.
options: Right: 21% is about one fifth.
One half would be 50%.
Three quarters is close to nitrogen's share, 78%.
One tenth would be 10%.

<math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>0.042</mn><mn>100</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{0.042}{100} \times 1{,}000{,}000</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>420</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>ppm</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 420\,\text{ppm}</annotation></semantics></math>. Share and importance are different. CO2 is only about 0.04% of air, yet it is the carbon source for photosynthesis, and it helps keep Earth warm (later topics in Unit 9 explain how).

CO2 is the raw material of photosynthesis, so it matters to every food chain.
Argon does nothing chemically, but that does not make every small gas unimportant.
Oxygen is about 21%; CO2 is about 0.04%.

why.correct: Uneven heating makes warm, light air rise near the equator and cooler, denser air sink elsewhere. The air moving between them is wind.
options: Right: unequal heating drives air to rise in some places and sink in others.
The Moon drives tides, not the global winds.
Mountains steer and lift wind locally, but they do not start global circulation.
Waves are made by wind, not the other way around.

why.correct: Air flowing toward the equator is deflected by Earth's rotation, the Coriolis effect: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, so a north wind becomes a northeast wind.
options: Right: the Coriolis effect turns the wind to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Sunlight heats air; it does not push it west.
There is no continuous mountain range along the equator.
Air at the equator rises; it draws air in from the north and south, and the turn comes from rotation.

why.correct: Moving air is turned to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, which is why the southern trade winds blow from the southeast.
options: Right: deflection is to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
Rightward deflection is the Northern Hemisphere pattern.
The Coriolis effect turns air sideways, not upward.
It acts in both hemispheres; only the direction of turning differs.

why.correct: Air that rose at the equator dropped its rain there. It sinks near 30°, warming as it falls, so it can hold more water and clouds rarely form.
options: Right: sinking, warming air makes the 30° latitudes dry.
Trade winds carry air, not most of the sand in the Sahara.
The most direct sunlight falls near the equator.
Air sinks at 30°; it rises near the equator and near 60°.

why.correct: Strong heating makes air rise near the equator. As it rises it cools, and its water vapor condenses into clouds and heavy rain.
options: Right: rising air at the equator brings heavy rain.
Air rises at the equator; sinking air is dry.
The westerlies blow between about 30° and 60°, not toward the equator.
Air at the equator rises strongly; it is far from still.

why.correct: The loop: heat, rise, rain, spread poleward aloft, sink near 30°, return along the surface as the trade winds.
Between 30° and 60° the surface winds blow from the west toward the east: the westerlies. They carry weather across most of the United States from west to east.
options: Right: the westerlies blow between 30° and 60°.
The trade winds blow between the equator and 30°.
The polar easterlies blow poleward of 60°.
The southeast trade winds are in the Southern Hemisphere, between the equator and 30° S.

why.correct: Rising air expands and cools, so its water vapor condenses into clouds and rain. Sinking air is compressed and warms, so clouds evaporate.
options: Right: rising means rain, sinking means dry.
The pattern is reversed: rising air cools, sinking air warms.
The equator gets the most sunlight and is very wet.
Air high up is dry; sinking air brings no rain.

why.correct: The trade winds blow from the east, toward the west, between about 30° N and the equator. Sailing ships went south first to catch them, then rode them west.
options: Right: the northeast trades push ships west below 30° N.
The westerlies blow toward the east, against a ship sailing west.
Going north of 60° is far out of the way, and the Caribbean is in the tropics.
The Caribbean is north of the equator, so crossing it is not needed.

why.correct: Between about 30° and 60° N the prevailing winds are the westerlies, so smoke, dust and storms usually move from west to east across North America.
options: Right: the westerlies move air eastward across the middle latitudes.
The trade winds blow from east to west, and only between the equator and 30°.
The Hadley cell lies between the equator and 30°.
The polar easterlies blow north of 60°.

why.correct: The 0-10° N bar is tallest, at 2,000 mm per year, where air rises near the equator.
options: Right: the band near the equator is the wettest.
20-30° N gets 450 mm, one of the driest bands, where air sinks.
40-60° N gets 1,000 mm, half as much as near the equator.
60-80° N gets 350 mm, the least.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mm</mtext></mrow><mrow><mn>450</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>mm</mtext></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2{,}000\,\text{mm}}{450\,\text{mm}}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">≈</mo><mn>4.4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 4.4</annotation></semantics></math> times. The mm cancel, so the answer has no unit.
Precipitation is high near the equator, low near 30°, higher again from 40-60° and low near the poles: wet where air rises, dry where it sinks.
options: Right: wet bands match rising air and dry bands sinking air.
This is reversed; sinking air brings dry weather.
Then every band would be wet, but 20-30° and 60-80° are dry.
The equator band is the wettest, which needs rising air there.

why.correct: Rain falls from 2,000 to 450 mm by 20-30° N, then rises to 1,000 mm at 40-60° N before falling again. The pattern is not a steady decline.
options: Right: rainfall rises again in the middle latitudes.
The 40-60° N band (1,000 mm) is wetter than the 20-30° N band (450 mm).
The driest band does not show a steady decline; the middle of the graph rises.
0-10° N gets 2,000 mm, more than 10-20° N (1,100 mm).

why.correct: Every link is needed: heating, rising and rain at the equator, dry air moving poleward aloft, and sinking, warming air near 30°.
A watershed (drainage basin) is an area of land: every drop that falls inside its divide runs off or flows underground toward the same body of water.
options: Right: a watershed is the land that drains to one body of water.
Water stored underground in rock and sediment is an aquifer, not a watershed.
A dam holds water, but a watershed is the land around it that drains in.
That is the river's mouth; the watershed is all the land upstream that drains to it.

why.correct: Water flows downhill, so the high ground between two valleys decides which way rain runs. That ridge line is the divide.
options: Right: a divide of high ground separates watersheds.
The main river runs through the middle of a watershed, not along its edge.
A dam sits across a river inside one watershed.
The water table is underground; watersheds are set by the land surface.

why.correct: Every stream in a watershed drains toward the same outlet. What enters a small stream upstream can be carried downstream to the town.
options: Right: tributaries carry pollutants downstream to the main river.
The waste is dumped into a stream, which flows on to the river.
Water evaporates, but most dissolved pollutants stay in the water.
Rivers flow downhill, away from their sources, toward the town.

why.correct: Forest soils, leaf litter and roots let rain soak in and slow its flow. Pavement and roofs shed water, so more runs off and reaches streams quickly, raising flood peaks.
options: Right: pavement turns rain into fast runoff.
Tree roots and leaf litter help water soak in, not block it.
The same rain can produce very different runoff depending on land cover.
Pavement blocks infiltration, so less water recharges groundwater.

why.correct: Water runs off steep ground quickly, with force to carry soil. Gentle slopes, permeable soil and plant cover let water soak in and hold soil in place.
options: Right: steep slopes speed up runoff and erosion.
On gentle slopes water moves slowly and has more time to soak in.
Sandy soil is permeable, so more water soaks in and less runs off.
Forest cover slows water and lets it soak in.

why.correct: A watershed is defined by the land surface and where it drains. An aquifer is underground: a layer of sand, gravel or rock whose pores hold groundwater. One region can contain both.
options: Right: a watershed is surface land; an aquifer is underground water storage.
This swaps the two definitions.
They are different: one is land surface, the other underground storage.
An aquifer is underground, not a river channel.

why.correct: The divide is the high ground. Rain on the far side runs downhill away from watershed A and into watershed B.
options: Right: water on the far side of the divide drains to watershed B.
Only rain inside the divide drains to watershed A's lake.
Water first runs downhill on the surface; the divide decides which watershed it joins.
Water on a slope moves downhill as runoff or infiltration.

why.correct: Water that soaks in moves down through soil until it reaches the water table, refilling the aquifer.
options: Right: infiltration recharges the aquifer.
Water soaking in moves down, not over the divide.
Runoff is water moving over the surface, the water that did not soak in.
The rock at the bottom of the diagram does not let water pass.

why.correct: Rain falling anywhere inside the divide either runs off to the stream or soaks down toward the aquifer, carrying whatever is on the land with it.
options: Right: the whole watershed feeds both the stream and the aquifer.
All the land inside the divide drains to the stream, not just the banks.
The diagram shows infiltration from the land surface recharging the aquifer.
Rain still reaches the stream as runoff from the rest of the watershed.

why.correct: South Creek had 55% runoff and 640 mg/L of sediment; North Creek had 10% runoff and 20 mg/L.
options: Right: the watershed with more runoff carried far more sediment.
The data show the opposite: more runoff, more sediment.
The forested North Creek had 10% runoff, the least.
640 mg/L is 32 times 20 mg/L.

<math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>55</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{55\%}{10\%} = 5.5</annotation></semantics></math> times.
South Creek is both paved or plowed and steep. Steep slopes also raise runoff and erosion, so the data cannot separate the two causes.

Both watersheds are 4 km².

why.correct: A solution fits the scenario (a field next to a stream) and says how it works: plants slow the water and roots hold the soil.
Watersheds nest. Everything that drains to Mill Creek then drains to the Ohio and then the Mississippi, so the creek's watershed lies inside the larger ones.
options: Right: small watersheds nest inside larger ones.
Mill Creek's water reaches the sea through the Mississippi, so it is not separate.
A tributary's watershed is smaller than the river basin it drains into.
A watershed is surface land, not an aquifer.

why.correct: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. As Earth orbits, each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun, getting more direct sunlight and longer days.
options: Right: the tilt makes each hemisphere lean toward or away from the Sun.
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter, so distance is not the cause.
The Sun's output barely changes over a year.
Earth spins at a steady rate; that makes day and night, not seasons.

why.correct: A beam of light that hits the surface head-on lights a small area; the same beam at a low angle spreads over a larger area, so each square meter gets less.
options: Right: the angle of the sunlight decides how concentrated it is.
The difference in distance is tiny compared with 150 million km.
Clouds matter locally, but the main cause is the angle of sunlight.
The equator has about 12 hours of daylight all year; the poles have long summer days, so day length is not the main cause.

why.correct: In June the North Pole leans toward the Sun, so the Northern Hemisphere has summer while the Southern Hemisphere, tilted away, has winter.
options: Right: the hemispheres have opposite seasons because of the tilt.
Both cities are the same distance from the Sun.
The Southern Hemisphere still gets sunlight; it is just less direct and for fewer hours.
Buenos Aires (35°) is closer to the equator than Chicago (42°), yet it is in winter.

why.correct: Albedo is reflectivity: fresh snow reflects most sunlight (high albedo); dark ocean water absorbs most of it (low albedo).
options: Right: albedo is the fraction or percent of sunlight reflected.
Heat given off is a separate process from reflecting sunlight.
The angle of sunlight is a different idea; it sets insolation.
Photosynthesis uses a small share of light; albedo is about reflection.

why.correct: Ice reflects most sunlight; ocean water absorbs most of it. Exposed water absorbs more energy, warms, and melts more ice: a loop that amplifies itself.
options: Right: losing bright ice lowers albedo and adds absorbed energy.
Open water has a lower albedo than ice, not higher.
Lower albedo means more sunlight absorbed, not less.
Melting ice absorbs heat; it does not release it.

why.correct: Snow reflects 85%, so it absorbs <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>85</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\% - 85\% = 15\%</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.15</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>300</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>W/m</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>W/m</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.15 \times 300\,\text{W/m}^{2} = 45\,\text{W/m}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Sunlight falls from 415 W/m² at the equator to 170 W/m² at the pole.
options: Right: the line falls with latitude.
The line slopes down, not up.
The values range from 415 to 170 W/m².
The pole has the lowest value, 170 W/m².

Sunlight at 60° N is about 43% less than at the equator.
The curve of Earth means sunlight hits high latitudes at a slant, spreading the same energy over a larger area.
options: Right: the angle of the sunlight explains the decrease.
All latitudes are essentially the same distance from the Sun.
A thinner atmosphere would block less light, not more.
High latitudes have very long days in summer.

why.correct: Abundant, steady insolation keeps the tropics warm year-round; low insolation keeps polar regions cold, giving tundra.
options: Right: insolation sets the temperature that shapes biomes.

Sunlight differs a lot with latitude, and temperature matters as much as rainfall.
The equator gets the most sunlight.

options: Right: the lowest albedo absorbs the most.
Fresh snow reflects the most (85%), so it absorbs the least.
Desert sand reflects 40%.
Grassland reflects 25%.

why.correct: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.12</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>200</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>W/m</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><msup><mtext>W/m</mtext><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.12 \times 200\,\text{W/m}^{2} = 24\,\text{W/m}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> reflected.
Dark evergreen trees stick up through the snow and absorb sunlight. Cleared land under snow is a bright surface with an albedo near 85%, so it reflects much more.
options: Right: open snow has a much higher albedo than forest.
In winter the grass is buried under snow, which reflects far more than forest.
Incoming sunlight is the same, but the share reflected changes.
Snow reflects most sunlight; its albedo is 85%.

why.correct: The tilt, not distance, changes how long the Sun is up and how high it climbs.

options: Right: at the equinoxes the tilt points neither pole at the Sun.
That is the case around June 21, northern summer.
That is the case around December 21, southern summer.
The tilt stays about 23.5° all year; only its direction relative to the Sun changes.

why.correct: Moist air drops its rain going up the windward side of a mountain. The air that comes down the leeward side is dry, so the land there is dry.
options: Right: the leeward side is the dry rain shadow.
The windward slope is wet; the rain shadow is on the other side.
A rain shadow is a dry region, not a shadow of light.
A rain shadow is a dry area beyond the range, not the peak.

why.correct: As air rises, the pressure on it drops, so it expands and cools. Cool air holds less water vapor, so clouds form and rain or snow falls.
options: Right: cooling of rising air causes condensation.
Soil temperature is not what makes clouds form.
Trees release water vapor; they do not pull it from the air.
Rising air expands; it is sinking air that is compressed.

why.correct: The trade winds and westerlies drag the surface water. The Coriolis effect and the continents in the way turn the moving water into large loops.
options: Right: winds push the surface water, and rotation and coastlines turn it into gyres.
Tides move water up and down the shore, not around ocean basins.
Rivers add water, but far too little to drive ocean-wide currents.
Volcanoes heat water locally; they do not drive basin-wide currents.

why.correct: The Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current carry warm water toward Europe, and westerly winds bring that mild ocean air over Britain. Calgary is far inland, where winters are much colder.
options: Right: warm water and maritime air moderate London's winters.
Both cities are at about 51° N.
A rain shadow makes a place dry; it does not explain cold winters.
Calgary is higher (about 1,000 m) than London, and London is the milder one.

why.correct: Water needs much more energy to change its temperature than rock and soil do. So the ocean stays cooler in summer and warmer in winter, and it moderates the air over nearby land.
options: Right: water changes temperature slowly, which moderates nearby climates.
Both get about the same sunlight at the same latitude.
The question compares towns at the same latitude.
Ocean air is milder in winter, but the cause is water's slow temperature change.

why.correct: In the troposphere air cools about 6.5 °C per kilometer of height. Kilimanjaro rises almost 5 km above the plains around it, so its peak is far colder.
options: Right: higher elevation means colder air.
The base and the peak are at the same latitude.
Glaciers form only where it is cold enough; many mountains have none.
The peak gets plenty of sunlight, often more than the base.

why.correct: The windward side faces the oncoming wind. Here the wind blows from the ocean, so the ocean-facing slope is windward.
options: Right: the windward side faces the wind coming off the ocean.
The side where air sinks is the leeward side.
The peak divides the two sides; it is not a side.
Only one side faces the wind.

why.correct: The air dropped most of its water on the windward side. Sinking down the leeward side, it is compressed and warms, so it can hold more water vapor and clouds rarely form.
options: Right: dry, warming air brings little rain to the leeward side.
Clouds form from moisture and rising air, not from sunlight blocked by mountains.
The wind keeps blowing from the ocean across the mountains.
Sinking air warms; it does not cool.

why.correct: Westerly winds bring moist air from the Pacific. It rises over the Sierra Nevada, drops rain and snow on the western slopes, and leaves the eastern side in a rain shadow.
options: Right: this is the rain shadow effect, with the wet side facing the Pacific.
Air rises on the windward (west) side and sinks on the east.
No ocean current flows between the slopes of a mountain range.
The dryness comes from the rain shadow, not from volcanoes.

The difference is 1,950 mm, which is large.
Dry Gulch gets far less, not more.

Fernvale's range is only <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mtext>°C</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17 - 5 = 12\,\text{°C}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Ocean air keeps Fernvale cooler in summer and warmer in winter. The mountains block that air from Dry Gulch, so its temperatures swing more, as inland climates do.
options: Right: the ocean moderates Fernvale's climate.
The caption says the towns are at about the same elevation.
The caption says they are at about the same latitude.
At the same latitude they get about the same sunlight.

why.correct: Mild, very wet Fernvale fits a temperate rainforest, like the coasts of the Pacific Northwest. Dry Gulch, with 250 mm a year, fits a desert or dry grassland.
options: Right: wet and mild on the coast, dry inland (a desert or dry grassland).
This swaps the two towns.

why.correct: Every link: westerly winds, rising and cooling on the west slope, rain there, dry sinking air on the east.

options: Right: a cold current makes the air above it cool and stable.
A cold current cools the air; it does not warm it.
Salt spray does not stop rain from forming.

why.correct: In an El Niño the trade winds weaken (or even reverse in places), so they stop holding warm water in the western Pacific.
options: Right: weaker trade winds mark an El Niño.
Stronger trade winds are a La Niña.
The trade winds blow toward the west and the equator; they do not turn toward the poles.
The change in the trade winds is what defines the event.

why.correct: The trade winds drag warm surface water away from South America toward the west. Cold, nutrient-rich water from below rises to take its place: upwelling.
options: Right: wind moves surface water away, and deep water rises to replace it.
Warm water is less dense, so it does not sink below cold water.
Rivers add only a little fresh water near their mouths.

why.correct: Weak upwelling brings fewer nutrients up. With less phytoplankton at the base of the food web, the anchovies and the animals that eat them decline.
options: Right: less upwelling means fewer nutrients, less plankton and less food.
El Niño makes the water off Peru warmer, not colder.
Trade winds weaken during El Niño.
Coastal rain does not make the open ocean fresh enough to kill fish.

why.correct: In La Niña the strong trade winds pile warm water and rising, rainy air even farther west, over Indonesia, while the cold eastern Pacific keeps Peru dry.
options: Right: La Niña makes the west wetter and the east drier.
That is the El Niño pattern.
La Niña brings extra rain to the western Pacific.
La Niña keeps the eastern Pacific cold and dry.

why.correct: ENSO swings between El Niño, neutral and La Niña every 2 to 7 years. The "Southern Oscillation" is the seesaw in air pressure between the western and eastern Pacific that goes with it.
options: Right: ENSO is a natural ocean-atmosphere cycle.
ENSO is natural and comes and goes; it has been recorded for centuries.
Currents around Antarctica are not ENSO.

why.correct: During El Niño, warm water that was piled up in the west spreads across the tropical Pacific surface, and that large warm surface gives heat to the atmosphere.
options: Right: a large warm ocean surface warms the air above it.
The extra warmth comes from heat moving from ocean to air, not a release of carbon dioxide from the seafloor.
ENSO has nothing to do with Earth's orbit.
ENSO is a tropical ocean and lower atmosphere cycle, not a stratosphere change.

why.correct: The El Niño map shows a long band of warmer-than-average water along the equator, warmest near Peru.
options: Right: the warm band runs along the equator to South America.
The far western Pacific is slightly cooler than average in the El Niño map.
The map shows the tropical Pacific, not the North Pacific.
The warm water is in the central and eastern Pacific.

why.correct: In La Niña the trade winds blow harder, pushing warm surface water west and pulling up more cold water off South America.
options: Right: strong trade winds and strong upwelling cool the east.
Weaker trade winds and warm water moving east describe El Niño.
There is no ice near Peru to cool the ocean.
Sunlight is similar across the tropical Pacific; winds explain the pattern.

why.correct: La Niña cools the water off Peru with strong upwelling, which brings nutrients up and supports large fish populations.
options: Right: La Niña brings stronger upwelling and more food for fish.
Moving to El Niño would weaken upwelling and cut the catch.
Warm water near Peru signals weak upwelling and fewer fish.
Weaker trade winds reduce upwelling.

why.correct: The trade winds control where the pool of warm water sits. When they weaken, it spreads east and the west cools a little; when they strengthen, it is pushed farther west.
options: Right: the same pool of warm water shifts east or west.
Both sides of the tropical Pacific are near the equator and share seasons.
Both maps show the band crossing the equator in the east and the west.
Volcanoes do not drive ENSO.

why.correct: In years 3 and 7 the water is warmest (about 23 °C) and the catch is smallest (1.8 and 2.4 million metric tons).
options: Right: warm years and low catches go together.
The warmest years have the lowest catches.
The two lines move in opposite directions.
The catch is about normal the year before each warm year and falls in the warm year itself.

An El Niño brings unusually warm water to the coast of Peru and weak upwelling. Years 3 and 7 have the highest temperatures and the lowest catches.
options: Right: the warm, low-catch years fit El Niño.
Year 5 is the coolest year with the biggest catch, more like La Niña.
Years 4 and 8 are near normal.
Years 2 and 6 are near normal.

why.correct: Weak trade winds and warmer-than-average water from the date line to South America, with rain in Peru and drought in Indonesia, are the signs of El Niño.
options: Right: these are El Niño conditions.
La Niña has stronger trade winds and cooler water in the eastern Pacific.
The bulletin describes winds and temperatures well away from normal.
A rain shadow is caused by mountains, not by Pacific winds.

why.correct: Warm water off South America means weak upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water, so less food for fish.
options: Right: warm water signals weak upwelling and fewer nutrients.
Drought in Indonesia is a separate effect, far from Peru.
Rain in the United States does not explain the fish catch.
How long conditions last does not explain why catches fall.

why.correct: Warm water feeds rising air and heavy rain. When El Niño moves the warm water east, the rain follows it toward Peru and leaves the western Pacific drier.
options: Right: the rain follows the warm water east.
The bulletin's two warnings only make sense if rain shifts, not if it stays even.
The warnings are for places thousands of kilometers apart, not one storm.
They are on opposite sides of the Pacific, not in one watershed.
